title: Potiphar's house (Genesis 39)
hookLine: a slave, falsely accused, and yet the Lord was with Joseph
last: THE PIT IS NOT THE END.

cards: Some people end up in work they never chose: a night shift taken because the rent was due, a first job in a city where they know no one, far below what they hoped for. Now make it far worse.
Joseph is barely more than a boy, in a foreign country, sold. He's a slave in the house of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard. Nobody from home knows where he is.
His father thinks he's dead. And the chapter's first line about him is not what you'd expect.

teach.h: WITH HIM, AND STILL A SLAVE.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian." Notice the order. The Lord was with him, and he was still in his master's house.
Being with God didn't mean getting out. It meant that where he was, things went well. Potiphar notices, and puts him in charge of everything he owns.
Then Potiphar's wife notices him too. Joseph is handsome, the text says, and day after day she presses him to sleep with her.

teach.h: HOW CAN I SIN AGAINST GOD?
teach.b: He refuses: his master has trusted him with everything, "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" One day, when the house is empty, she grabs his garment. He runs, and leaves it in her hand.
His brothers stripped off one garment; now another is left behind, and again clothing is used to tell a lie. She tells the household, then her husband, that Joseph attacked her.
Potiphar is furious, and Joseph is thrown into prison. He did the right thing and lost everything again. Then the chapter repeats itself: "But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy."
The keeper of the prison puts him in charge of the other prisoners.
Twice in one chapter, from the top of a house to the bottom of a prison, the same line.
It doesn't promise Joseph safety. It says, twice, that he wasn't alone where he landed.

how: Many Christians turn to Genesis 39 in seasons of unfair treatment or unwanted work, and the repeated line "the LORD was with Joseph" is often used in sermons and devotions about God's presence in hard places.

games.q: you're Joseph. your master trusts you with everything. his wife keeps pressing you, and today she grabs your garment in an empty house. what do you do?
o: stay and try to talk her out of it.
run, and leave the garment in her hand.

games.why: he runs and leaves it behind. she uses the garment to accuse him, and he ends up in prison. doing right cost him everything, again.

practice: Find a place in your life you'd leave if you could, a job, a role, a situation that isn't fair, and one small piece of it you could do well anyway, with care, not for anyone's praise. Picture doing it.
If you pray, you can ask God to be with you there; if you don't, notice that you can bring something good into a place you didn't choose.

wordCard.voice: Potiphar's house. Where Joseph served as a slave, rose to run everything, refused his master's wife, and was falsely accused.

orig.note: Hebrew: prospering, making things succeed. Genesis uses this root for Joseph in Potiphar's house and in prison.
